lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4, what did a bulb need to light up? (A complete loop, with no gap and the switch closed.) Now you will draw circuits with symbols and build two kinds: series and parallel.

Scientists draw circuits with symbols, so anyone can read them. Wires are straight lines. A cell is a long line (+) and a short, thick one (−); two or more make a battery. A lamp is a circle with a cross; a motor, a circle with M.

Stay safe: mains electricity from sockets is strong enough to badly hurt you. Never poke anything into a socket, keep water and wet hands away from plugs, and keep away from power lines. If a button battery is swallowed, tell a grown-up at once.

In a series circuit everything is in one loop. Add a lamp and they all glow more dimly; if one breaks, they all go out. More cells push harder: the push is the voltage, in volts (V). One cell is about 1.5 V.

In a parallel circuit the electricity has more than one path. Each lamp has its own branch, so it glows as brightly as a lamp on its own. If one breaks, the others stay lit. Homes are wired in parallel.
A switch in one branch turns only that branch on and off. A switch before the paths split turns everything off. Here the switch in lamp A's branch is open, so lamp A is off, but lamp B still lights.

On this unit's page, tap TRY IT IN THE LAB: close the switch, then take out a wire to make a gap. Add a second bulb: two bulbs in one loop share the cell's push, so both glow more dimly, just like a series circuit.

Try it in the world: count the light switches at home: each light has its own, because homes are wired in parallel. Then draw a torch's circuit with symbols. Next, in grade 8: circuits, current and voltage.

exercises.prompt: Which part does this symbol stand for?
exercises.hint: Think of a bulb's glowing wire: a cross inside a circle.
exercises.explain: A circle with a cross is a lamp (bulb).

exercises.prompt: In a series circuit, all the parts are in one loop.
exercises.explain: True: a series circuit has one loop, and the electricity flows through every part in turn.

exercises.prompt: What must you never do with a plug socket?
exercises.hint: Mains electricity is strong enough to badly hurt you.
exercises.explain: Never poke anything into a socket: mains electricity can badly hurt you.
choices: ask a grown-up to plug a lamp in

exercises.prompt: The switch is closed. How many lamps light?
exercises.explain: The switch is closed, so the one loop is complete and both lamps light.

exercises.prompt: Two or more cells joined together make a battery.
exercises.hint: Look at the battery symbol: how many cells?
exercises.explain: True: a battery is two or more cells joined together.

exercises.prompt: One lamp in a series circuit breaks. What happens to the other lamps?
exercises.hint: A broken lamp makes a gap in the only loop.
exercises.explain: The broken lamp leaves a gap in the only loop, so every lamp goes out.

exercises.prompt: What kind of circuit is this?
exercises.hint: Count the paths from the cell and back.
exercises.explain: Each lamp has its own branch: more than one path, so it is a parallel circuit.

exercises.prompt: Lamp B lights, even though the switch in lamp A's branch is open.
exercises.hint: Does lamp B's branch have a gap?
exercises.explain: True: lamp B has its own complete path, so the open switch in A's branch does not stop it.

exercises.hint: Series is one path; parallel is several branches.
exercises.explain: Series: one loop; all go out together; more lamps, dimmer. Parallel: several paths; own switches; homes.
items: one lamp breaks, all go out
each light has its own switch

exercises.prompt: This lamp has two cells. Compared with one cell, how does it glow?
exercises.hint: Two cells push harder than one.
exercises.explain: Two cells give a bigger push (a higher voltage), so the lamp glows more brightly.

exercises.prompt: Match each part to its symbol.
exercises.hint: Picture each real part, then its simple drawing.
exercises.explain: Lamp: a circle with a cross. Cell: a long and a short line. Motor: a circle with M. Open switch: a lifted line.
matches: a long and a short line

exercises.prompt: A buzzer sounds louder when you add more cells.
exercises.hint: More cells give a bigger push.
exercises.explain: True: more cells push harder, so a buzzer sounds louder and a lamp glows brighter.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order to build a circuit with a lamp and a switch.
exercises.hint: Make one complete loop from the cell and back, then close the gap.
exercises.explain: The cell, a wire to the lamp, the lamp to the switch, back to the cell, then close the switch to complete the loop.
items: Join a wire from + to the lamp
Join the lamp to the switch
Put a cell in its holder

exercises.prompt: The main switch is closed. How many of the three lamps light?
exercises.hint: Check each branch for an open switch.
exercises.explain: The first two branches are complete paths; the third branch's switch is open. So 2 lamps light.

exercises.prompt: Why are homes wired in parallel, not in series?
exercises.hint: Think about what happens when you switch off one room's light.
exercises.explain: In parallel each light has its own path and switch; in series one switch or broken bulb would turn off every light.
choices: So each light can be switched on its own.
So one broken bulb turns all off.

exercises.prompt: Tilly adds a third lamp to her series circuit. What happens?
exercises.hint: In series, the lamps share the cell's push.
exercises.explain: Three lamps share one cell's push in one loop, so each glows more dimly.

exercises.prompt: If a button battery is swallowed, it is fine to wait and see.
exercises.hint: Button batteries can burn the inside of the body quickly.
exercises.explain: False: tell a grown-up at once and get help straight away. Keep button batteries away from little children.

exercises.prompt: What happens when the main switch is open?
exercises.hint: The main switch is on the path every branch shares.
exercises.explain: The main switch is before the paths split, so opening it breaks every path: both lamps go out.

exercises.prompt: A toy needs 6 V. Each cell gives 1.5 V. How many cells must be joined in series?
exercises.hint: Cells in series add their voltages. How many lots of 1.5 make 6?
exercises.explain: Cells in series add up their push: 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6. 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 cells, which together make a battery.
